-description: Decompose batches of RHAISTRAT strategies into implementation epic DAGs. Accepts explicit IDs or a JQL query. Non-interactive.

+description: Decompose batches of RHAISTRAT strategies into implementation epic DAGs. Use when given RHAISTRAT strategy IDs or a JQL query selecting strategies to decompose into epics. Accepts explicit IDs or a JQL query. Non-interactive.
- Priority inheritance: prerequisite epic inherits the highest priority of all HLRs it transitively enables
- An epic blocking all P0 work is implicitly P0

-- Priority split: when an epic maps to HLRs at multiple priority levels, check whether the lower-priority HLRs represent distinct, deferrable features. A feature is "distinct and deferrable" only when it could ship as its own epic with independent user value AND does not share data structures, UI surfaces, or API endpoints with the P0 work. If yes, split them into separate epics by priority so each can be planned independently. If the lower-priority HLR is incidental to the P0 work (error handling, doc coverage, config override that falls out of the same implementation) or is tightly coupled to the same implementation surface, keep it bundled — splitting tightly coupled work creates duplication and artificial boundaries.

+- Priority split: when an epic maps to HLRs at multiple priority levels, check whether the lower-priority HLRs represent distinct, deferrable features. A feature is "distinct and deferrable" only when it could ship as its own epic with independent user value AND does not share data structures, UI surfaces, or API endpoints with the P0 work. If yes, split them into separate epics by priority so each can be planned independently. If the lower-priority HLR is incidental to the P0 work (error handling, doc coverage, config override that falls out of the same implementation) or is tightly coupled to the same implementation surface, keep it bundled — splitting tightly coupled work creates duplication and artificial boundaries. When you keep a lower-priority HLR bundled, record the bundling where the mapping is read: in the HLR Traceability Matrix, flag that HLR's row as `bundled` and state inline why it is not separately schedulable (it edits the same call sites, data structure, or surface as the higher-priority work — splitting would double-touch them). The row-level flag is what shows a reviewer the priority label was analyzed rather than collapsed; a rationale that lives only in a distant prose section does not.

- **Redundant / overlapping HLRs — consolidate, never split:** strategies merged from multiple sources sometimes state one capability twice in different words (e.g. "select two or more runs and view their parameters and metrics side by side" and "a diff view highlighting which parameters and metrics changed between two selected runs" — the diff view is a presentation mode of the same comparison surface over the same run data). When two HLRs describe the same data structure, UI surface, or API endpoint for the same component and team — one a restatement or presentation mode of the other — they are ONE capability: cover both with a single epic whose HLR Traceability lists both HLR ids, at the higher of the two priorities. Do not split them into separate epics by priority label: on a shared surface a P0/P1 pair is redundant wording, not a deferral signal, and splitting produces two epics building the same surface plus an artificial serialization edge between them — a boundary violation even when the second epic only extends the first's surface.

- `docs-authoring` priority exception: `docs-authoring` epics are exempt from priority inheritance. They do not push their priority upstream to the implementations they depend on. Instead, derive their priority from the strategy frontmatter `priority` field: Critical→P0, Major→P1, Normal/Minor/Undefined→P2. If the field is missing or empty, default to P2.
- Priority inversions (P0/P1/P2 inconsistent with technical complexity/reliability)
- Scope traps: ACs implying infrastructure that doesn't exist, contradictions between out-of-scope items and NFRs, storage beyond design intent

+- Epic size overages kept deliberately: when you keep an epic above the ~2-week guideline because it is one logical change (a split would duplicate an audit or fragment a single mechanical pass over one surface), the Health Warning must carry a **re-split trigger** — the concrete, measurable planning condition under which the epic should be re-split (e.g. "re-split along sub-system lines if the call-site audit finds materially more sites than the estimate"). A justified overage with a recorded trigger is a managed trade-off; a bare "above guideline, noted for planning awareness" note is an unresolved defect that the review will dock and the contract validator will flag.

Every `VIOLATION:` line MUST become an entry in your `issues` list (use the violation text as the description) AND must zero the criterion it maps to, per the rule that critical/major issues force 0:
- priority inheritance (lower-priority epic blocking P0 work) → severity major, criterion "HLR Coverage"

- parallel edge (Rules 7/8/10 — a `dependencies` edge between implementation types that must run parallel) → severity critical, criterion "DAG Coherence" (the edge serializes work the ordering rules mandate as parallel; there is no component-scope or artifact-dependency exemption)

The issue must still appear in the `issues` list with the correction named ("record the concrete re-split trigger in the Health Warning") so the unconditional revision applies it.

- **0**: Epics violate the component/team boundary rule (work for different teams bundled into one epic), or an epic is clearly oversized (multiple sprints of work).

-Check: For each epic, verify component and team fields. Look for epics that bundle work across multiple components or teams. **Also check for scope duplication across sibling epics:** compare the scope sections and acceptance criteria of all epics. If two or more epics independently build the same data structure, UI surface, API endpoint, or component (e.g., both create a benchmark list with status indicators, or both implement log viewing against the same endpoint), that is a major issue — it means the boundary was drawn incorrectly and the epics should be merged or re-split along a different axis. Minor incidental overlap (e.g., both epics mention the same config value) is not duplication. **A split that puts two presentation modes of ONE surface in two epics is duplication even though neither epic rebuilds the other's work** — e.g., a P0 epic building a side-by-side comparison view and a P1 epic building a diff view of the same data for the same team: the diff view is a thin increment on the first epic's surface, not an independent deliverable, and the correct shape is ONE epic whose HLR Traceability lists both HLRs. A priority-label difference (P0 vs P1) on the same surface is redundant requirement wording, not a boundary — flag the split as a major issue. **Also check for work-product type mixing:** if a single epic bundles code implementation with content authoring (sample notebooks, tutorials, curated examples), flag as a major issue — these are different kinds of work with different review criteria and should be separate epics even when owned by the same team.

A split demand on that shape produces churn without resolving the overage (the split executes, the epic stays above guideline, and the restructuring can inject new defects). Instead record the overage as a minor issue (watch item) that names a **re-split trigger**: the measurable planning condition under which the epic should be re-split (e.g. "if the campaign outgrows a sprint of effort, split the rollout work out along environment-setup lines"). With a trigger on the record — in the decomposition's Health Warnings or in the issue itself — the overage is a managed trade-off and this criterion still scores 2; do not dock the criterion for a triggered, justified overage. An overage acknowledged with no trigger anywhere (a bare "flagged for planning awareness only" note) scores 1, with the named correction "record the concrete re-split trigger". The carve-out does not apply to genuine boundary violations: an epic spanning multiple sprints of heterogeneous work, or mixing work streams that warrant separate review cycles, is oversized — demand the split (major issue) per the base rubric.
- **Multi-component/team epic**: Split into separate epics per the component/team tuple rule. Assign new epic IDs continuing the sequence (e.g., if last epic is E007, new ones are E008, E009).
- **Oversized epic**: Split by sub-deliverable into smaller epics.

+- **Oversized epic that is one logical change (missing re-split trigger)**: when the review names a missing re-split trigger, or flags an overage on an epic that is a single mechanical pass over one surface / one audit (a split would duplicate the audit or fragment the change), do NOT split — add the concrete re-split trigger to the summary's Health Warning: the measurable planning condition under which the epic should be re-split (e.g. "re-split along sub-system lines if the audit finds materially more sites than the estimate"). Splitting this shape leaves the overage unresolved and injects new defects (unjustified edges, stale epic counts in the summary); the trigger converts the overage into a managed trade-off.
